questions.title: Viewing leaf cells
questions.stem: A student observes leaf cells with a light microscope. A drawing of one cell is 36 mm long. The actual cell is 0.09 mm long.

parts.q: Name the structure that contains genetic material and the structure where photosynthesis occurs.
ms: Nucleus (1).
Chloroplast (1).

parts.q: Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Show your working.
ms: Magnification = image size / actual size (1).

parts.q: Describe how to prepare a thin leaf sample on a microscope slide.
ms: Place a thin sample in a drop of water on a slide (1).
Lower a coverslip gently at an angle to reduce trapped air (1).
Remove excess water and begin observing with low-power objective (1).

parts.q: Give three differences between a bacterial cell and a leaf cell.
ms: Bacteria lack a nucleus; leaf cells have one (1).
Bacteria have no chloroplasts; photosynthetic leaf cells have chloroplasts (1).
Bacteria have no mitochondria; leaf cells have mitochondria (1). Accept bacterial circular DNA/plasmids versus chromosomes in a nucleus as an alternative distinct difference.

parts.q: Calculate the increase in mass of the cylinder in water.
Calculate the percentage increase in mass of this cylinder.
Explain why the cylinder in concentrated sugar solution loses mass.
ms: Water moves out of potato cells (1).
Through partially permeable membranes (1).
By osmosis, from a more dilute solution inside to a more concentrated solution outside (1).

parts.q: Describe three controls or improvements that make this comparison more reliable.
ms: Use cylinders of equal dimensions/from the same potato (1).
Use the same immersion time and temperature (1).
Repeat with several cylinders and calculate means; or blot each cylinder consistently before weighing (1).

questions.title: Enzymes and digestion
questions.stem: Amylase digests starch. In a test at 35 °C, starch takes 120 seconds to disappear. At 45 °C it takes 60 seconds.

parts.q: Name the product type made by amylase and the reagent used to test for starch.
ms: Sugars (1).
Iodine solution (1).

parts.q: Calculate the ratio of the time at 35 °C to the time at 45 °C. Give the simplest whole-number ratio.
Explain how bile helps the digestion of fats.
ms: Neutralises stomach acid in the small intestine (1).
Provides alkaline conditions for enzymes (1).
Emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing surface area for lipase (1).

parts.q: Explain why amylase works very slowly at 80 °C.
ms: High temperature changes the shape of the enzyme/active site (1).
The substrate no longer fits the active site (1).
The enzyme is denatured, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form (1).

questions.title: Transport in the body
questions.stem: Blood circulates between the heart, lungs and body tissues.

parts.q: Name the blood component that carries oxygen and the component involved in clotting.
ms: Red blood cells (1).
Platelets (1).

parts.q: Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle.
ms: Left ventricle pumps blood around the whole body (1).
Needs to generate higher pressure than the right ventricle, which pumps to nearby lungs (1).

parts.q: Explain three features of alveoli that make gas exchange effective.
ms: Large surface area increases exchange (1).
Thin walls provide short diffusion distance (1).
Good blood supply/ventilation maintains a concentration gradient (1).

parts.q: Describe how coronary heart disease develops and one treatment.
ms: Fatty deposits build up in coronary arteries (1).
Reduced blood flow reduces oxygen supply to heart muscle (1).
Stent holds artery open or statins lower blood cholesterol and slow deposit formation (1).

questions.title: Preventing infectious disease
questions.stem: A school has 800 pupils. Following a vaccination programme, 680 pupils are vaccinated.

parts.q: Calculate the percentage of pupils vaccinated.
State one bacterial disease and one viral disease from the course.
ms: Salmonella food poisoning or gonorrhoea (1).
Measles, HIV or tobacco mosaic virus (1).

parts.q: Explain how vaccination reduces the risk of becoming ill after later exposure to a pathogen.
ms: Vaccine introduces dead/inactive pathogen or pathogen antigens.
Antigens stimulate white blood cells.
White blood cells produce specific antibodies.
Some white blood cells remain as memory cells.
On later exposure the specific antibodies are produced faster.
Antibodies destroy the pathogen before it causes serious illness. Accept a valid explanation of reduced transmission protecting unvaccinated people as an alternative final point.
parts.note: Award one mark for each distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.

parts.q: Name the gas in the bubbles and the organelle that absorbs light.
ms: Oxygen (1).
Chloroplast (1).

parts.q: Calculate the decrease in bubbles per minute between 10 cm and 30 cm.
ms: 32 bubbles per minute (1).

parts.q: Explain the pattern in the table.
ms: Light intensity decreases as lamp distance increases (1).
Less light energy is available for photosynthesis (1).
Photosynthesis rate decreases, so fewer oxygen bubbles are produced each minute (1).

parts.q: Suggest three improvements to the method.
ms: Collect gas volume rather than count unequal bubbles (1).
Keep temperature constant using a water bath/heat shield (1).
Repeat each distance and calculate a mean; or control carbon dioxide with the same bicarbonate solution (1).

questions.title: Respiration during exercise
questions.stem: A runner starts a fast sprint. Their muscles need more energy.

parts.q: Complete the word equation for aerobic respiration: glucose + ____ → ____ + water.
ms: Oxygen (1).
Carbon dioxide (1).

parts.q: State two changes to the body during exercise that deliver more oxygen to muscles.
ms: Heart rate increases (1).
Breathing rate and/or depth increases (1).

parts.q: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in human muscles.
ms: Aerobic uses oxygen; anaerobic does not (1).
Anaerobic forms lactic acid; aerobic forms carbon dioxide and water (1).
Anaerobic transfers less energy per glucose molecule (1).

parts.q: Explain why breathing remains fast for a while after the sprint.
ms: Lactic acid accumulated when oxygen supply was insufficient (1).
Extra oxygen is needed to react with/remove accumulated lactic acid (1).
This extra oxygen requirement is the oxygen debt (1).

questions.title: Comparing antiseptics
questions.stem: Students use a teacher-approved bacterial culture on agar. Equal paper discs contain antiseptic A, antiseptic B or sterile water. Mean clear-zone diameters are A: 12 mm; B: 8 mm; water: 0 mm.

parts.q: Explain why the agar and inoculating equipment should be sterile.
ms: Sterilisation removes unwanted microorganisms.
This reduces contamination so growth reflects the intended bacterial culture.

parts.q: Give two controlled variables, other than disc size.
ms: Use the same bacterial species / starting concentration.
Keep agar depth, incubation temperature or incubation time the same (one additional valid control).

parts.q: Use π = 3.14 to calculate the area of A’s clear circular zone.
ms: Radius = 12/2 = 6 mm.
Area = πr² = 3.14 × 36.
Area = 113.04 mm².

parts.q: State a conclusion, its supporting evidence, and one reason to repeat the investigation.
ms: A inhibits growth more than B under the tested conditions.
A has a larger clear zone than B; the water control has none.
Repeats allow a mean and identification of variation / anomalous results.

questions.title: Investigating yellow leaves
questions.stem: Tomato plants have yellow leaves and slow growth. No pathogen has yet been identified. Group 1 receives a complete mineral solution; group 2 receives an identical solution without magnesium. All other conditions are kept equal.

parts.q: Explain why a yellow leaf does not by itself prove infection.
ms: Several conditions can cause yellowing.
A mineral deficiency rather than a pathogen may be responsible.

parts.q: Explain why lacking magnesium can reduce growth.
ms: Magnesium is required for chlorophyll production.
Less chlorophyll reduces light absorption / photosynthesis.
Less glucose is available to make biomass / support growth.

parts.q: State three controls for the comparison.
ms: Use the same plant species and similar starting age / size.
Provide the same light and temperature (one valid environmental control).
Provide equal solution volumes and all other mineral concentrations.

parts.q: Suggest a useful additional diagnostic method and explain its purpose.
ms: Use a suitable laboratory test / pathogen identification or validated antibody test.
It can identify or provide evidence of a particular pathogen rather than relying on symptoms alone.

questions.title: Defending plants
questions.stem: A leaf-eating mammal attacks plants with soft leaves. A second plant has thorns and contains a toxic chemical. A third plant has damaged bark and a fungal infection.

parts.q: Explain how thorns and a toxic chemical can reduce damage.
ms: Thorns can deter or injure herbivores, reducing feeding.
Toxic chemicals can poison / deter herbivores.
Reduced feeding preserves tissues needed for growth / photosynthesis.

parts.q: Describe two physical barriers, other than thorns, and explain one of their effects.
ms: Cellulose cell walls provide a physical barrier.
Waxy cuticle or bark provides another physical barrier.
A barrier reduces pathogen entry into plant tissues.

parts.q: Explain why bark damage can increase infection risk.
ms: Damage breaches a physical barrier.
Fungal pathogens can enter exposed tissues more easily.

parts.q: Give two ways a plant can defend itself after infection or attack.
ms: Produce antibacterial chemicals / defensive poisons.
Shed infected leaves or use another valid specified defence such as curling leaves.

questions.title: Exchange surfaces and cell size
questions.stem: Model cells are cubes. Cube A has side length 1 mm; cube B has side length 3 mm. Surface area of a cube = 6 × side²; volume = side³.

parts.q: Calculate the surface-area-to-volume ratio of cube B.
ms: Surface area = 6 x 9 = 54 mm² (1).
Volume = 27 mm³ (1).

parts.q: Explain why diffusion alone may be insufficient for a large multicellular organism.
ms: Smaller surface-area-to-volume ratio than a small organism (1).
Longer internal diffusion distances (1).
Diffusion cannot supply all cells rapidly enough to meet demand for oxygen/nutrients (1).

parts.q: A micrograph is 72 mm wide at ×600. Calculate the real width in micrometres.
ms: 120 micrometres (1).

parts.q: Explain how active transport differs from diffusion.
ms: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient; diffusion is down it (1).
Active transport requires energy from respiration; diffusion does not (1).

Equal average rates produce no net transfer (1).

Reduces bias caused by measuring surface solution rather than tissue mass (1). Accept another coherent error-improvement-benefit sequence.

ms: Changes in pH can alter the active-site shape (1).
Substrate becomes less complementary (1).
Fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form; sufficiently extreme pH can denature the enzyme (1).

parts.q: Explain why temperature, enzyme concentration and starch concentration must each be controlled.
ms: Temperature affects collision rate/denaturation (1).
Enzyme concentration affects the number of available active sites (1).
Starch concentration affects collision frequency/substrate availability, so changes could confound the pH comparison (1).

questions.title: Heart disease and evidence
questions.stem: In a study, 18 of 300 people in group A developed heart disease, compared with 45 of 300 in group B. Group A took part in an exercise programme. The groups were not randomly allocated.

parts.q: Calculate the percentage developing heart disease in group A.
Explain why the study does not prove that exercise alone caused the difference.
ms: Groups may differ in other risk factors such as diet/smoking/age (1).
These confounding factors could explain part/all of the difference (1).

parts.q: Explain how the heart and blood vessels maintain effective delivery of oxygen to body tissues.
ms: Double circulation sends blood to lungs and then to body.
Right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to lungs.
Oxygen enters blood at alveoli.
Left ventricle produces high pressure for circulation to body tissues.
Arteries carry blood away from heart and withstand high pressure.
Capillaries have thin walls enabling short diffusion distance into tissues. Accept valves preventing backflow or red cells carrying oxygen using haemoglobin as alternative relevant points.
parts.note: Award one mark per distinct relevant linked point, maximum 6.

questions.title: Infection and immunity
questions.stem: A viral infection causes symptoms in some patients. A doctor explains that antibiotics will not cure the viral infection.

parts.q: Explain why antibiotics are ineffective against viruses.
ms: Antibiotics target bacterial structures/processes (1).
Viruses reproduce inside host cells and do not have the same targets (1).

parts.q: Describe three ways white blood cells defend the body against pathogens.
ms: Phagocytosis/engulfing pathogens (1).
Producing specific antibodies (1).
Producing antitoxins to neutralise toxins (1).

parts.q: Explain how antibiotic resistance can increase in a bacterial population.
ms: Mutation produces a resistant bacterium/variation already exists (1).
Antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria, leaving resistant bacteria (1).
Resistant bacteria reproduce and pass on resistance, increasing its frequency (1).

parts.q: Give two reasons why a new drug is tested before use in patients.
ms: Determine toxicity/safety (1).
Determine effectiveness or an appropriate dose (1).

questions.title: Limiting photosynthesis
questions.stem: At a fixed temperature, a plant absorbs 2.4 mg of carbon dioxide in 4 minutes at light setting A and 4.8 mg in 4 minutes at setting B. Doubling the light again gives no further increase.

parts.q: Calculate the carbon dioxide uptake rate at setting B.
Calculate the percentage increase in uptake from A to B.
Explain why doubling light beyond B may give no further increase.
ms: Light is no longer the limiting factor (1).
Carbon dioxide concentration or temperature may limit the rate (1).
Increasing that limiting factor, within a suitable range, would allow rate to increase (1).

parts.q: A grower proposes heating the greenhouse all night to increase photosynthesis. Evaluate this proposal.
ms: No photosynthesis without light at night (1).
Heating costs money/energy and may not raise yield enough to cover costs (1).
It may be useful only with lighting and sufficient carbon dioxide, or for preventing cold damage; conclusion must link to conditions (1).

questions.title: Metabolism and exercise
questions.stem: A person runs at increasing speed until oxygen delivery can no longer meet demand.

parts.q: Explain the relationship between respiration and metabolism.
ms: Respiration transfers energy from glucose (1).
This energy supports metabolic reactions such as protein synthesis or conversion of glucose to glycogen (1).

parts.q: Explain why anaerobic respiration leads to muscle fatigue and an oxygen debt.
ms: Glucose is incompletely broken down to lactic acid (1).
Lactic acid accumulation contributes to fatigue (1).
Extra oxygen is required after exercise to react with/remove the lactic acid (1).

parts.q: Describe how lactic acid is processed after exercise.
ms: Transported in blood from muscles to liver (1).
Converted back into glucose in the liver (1).
Oxygen/energy is required during recovery; accept some glucose stored as glycogen (1).

parts.q: Compare anaerobic respiration in yeast with that in muscles.
ms: Yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscles produce lactic acid (1).
Both transfer energy without oxygen/from incomplete breakdown of glucose (1).

questions.title: Assessing an antiseptic claim
questions.stem: An antiseptic company compares equal discs on agar seeded with one approved bacterial strain. Mean inhibition diameters are control: 6 mm; low concentration: 10 mm; high concentration: 14 mm. All discs are 6 mm wide. The company claims its product kills every type of pathogen.

parts.q: Calculate the clear-zone area outside the high-concentration disc, using π = 3.14.
ms: Outer radius = 7 mm and disc radius = 3 mm.
Subtract areas: π(7² − 3²).
Area = 125.6 mm².

parts.q: Explain why the claim is not justified.
ms: Only one bacterial strain was tested, not every pathogen.
Inhibition of visible growth does not prove all cells were killed.
The claim extends beyond the experimental conditions / ignores viruses, fungi or other untested pathogens.

parts.q: Describe two precautions that reduce contamination and one school incubation precaution.
ms: Sterilise medium / equipment.
Open lids briefly and use aseptic inoculation.
Incubate at 25°C and do not reopen incubated plates.

parts.q: Why report several independent plates rather than a single plate?
ms: To assess variation and improve reliability of a mean.

questions.title: Targeted antibody delivery
questions.stem: A tumour has antigen X on many of its cells. Scientists make a monoclonal antibody against X and attach a drug. In a trial, 42 of 70 treated patients improve, compared with 21 of 70 receiving the comparison treatment.

parts.q: Describe how a hybridoma producing the antibody is made.
ms: Expose a mouse to the antigen and obtain antibody-producing lymphocytes.
Fuse lymphocytes with tumour cells.
Select and clone a suitable hybridoma to produce identical antibodies.

parts.q: Explain the advantage of attaching the drug to this antibody.
ms: The antibody binds specifically to antigen X.
Attached drug is delivered to antigen-bearing target cells.
This may reduce exposure / damage to healthy cells compared with non-targeted delivery.

parts.q: Calculate the difference in improvement percentage points.
ms: Comparison: 21/70 × 100 = 30%.
Difference = 30 percentage points.

parts.q: Give one reason the improvement data alone do not establish that the treatment is preferable.
ms: Side effects, long-term outcome, cost or comparable trial design must also be evaluated.

questions.title: Diagnosing a crop problem
questions.stem: A crop has yellow leaves. Some plants also have black spots. An agronomist compares magnesium content, performs a pathogen test and investigates whether spraying a fungicide improves growth.

parts.q: Distinguish two possible causes of yellow leaves and explain a growth effect.
ms: Magnesium deficiency can reduce chlorophyll.
A pathogen can damage photosynthetic tissue.
Either can reduce photosynthesis and glucose available for growth.

parts.q: Explain why a positive pathogen test does not prove every yellow leaf is caused only by that pathogen.
ms: The test identifies presence / a marker, not all causes of every symptom.
Mineral deficiency or other environmental causes may coexist.

parts.q: Design a controlled comparison of the fungicide’s effect.
ms: Randomly allocate similar affected plants to fungicide and control groups.
Keep nutrient supply, light, water and other conditions constant.
Repeat with enough plants and compare mean growth using the same measurement interval.

parts.q: Explain how an intact cuticle and a defensive chemical can help plants.
ms: A cuticle reduces pathogen entry as a physical barrier.
A defensive chemical can inhibit microbes or deter herbivores.

questions.title: Reflexes and reaction time
questions.stem: Five ruler-drop distances are 16, 18, 15, 17 and 19 cm.

parts.q: Calculate the mean distance.
ms: Sum = 85 cm (1).

parts.q: Name the type of cell that detects a stimulus and the type of cell that carries an impulse to a muscle.
ms: Receptor (1).
Motor neurone (1).

parts.q: Describe the route taken by an impulse in a reflex arc from a receptor to a muscle.
ms: Sensory neurone carries impulse to central nervous system (1).
Relay neurone passes impulse within CNS (1).
Motor neurone carries impulse to the muscle/effector (1).

parts.q: Explain three controls or improvements in a ruler-drop investigation.
ms: Same starting position/zero aligned with fingers (1).
Same hand/person and posture when comparing conditions (1).
Repeat and calculate mean; avoid cues by varying delay before release (one valid improvement for 1).

questions.title: Blood glucose control
questions.stem: After a meal, blood glucose concentration rises.

parts.q: Name the organ that produces insulin and state how insulin travels to target organs.
ms: Pancreas (1).
In the blood (1).

parts.q: State two effects of insulin that reduce blood glucose concentration.
ms: Glucose moves from blood into cells (1).
Glucose is converted to glycogen in liver/muscles (1).

parts.q: Compare Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes.
ms: Type 1 pancreas produces little/no insulin (1).
Type 2 body cells respond less effectively to insulin (1).
Type 1 often treated with insulin injections; Type 2 often managed with controlled carbohydrate diet and exercise (1).

parts.q: Explain why a person with diabetes should use several blood glucose readings rather than one reading to judge control.
ms: Glucose changes during the day (1).
Meals/exercise affect readings (1).
Several readings reveal patterns and reduce the influence of an unusual reading (1).

questions.title: Hormones and reproduction
questions.stem: Hormones coordinate the menstrual cycle.

parts.q: State where oestrogen is mainly produced and one of its roles in the menstrual cycle.
ms: Ovaries (1).
Builds/thickens uterus lining (1).

parts.q: Name the hormone that causes ovulation and the hormone that stimulates egg maturation.
ms: LH causes ovulation (1).
FSH stimulates egg maturation (1).

parts.q: Explain three ways contraception can prevent pregnancy.
ms: Barrier method: a condom or diaphragm forms a physical barrier.
The barrier prevents sperm reaching the egg, so fertilisation cannot occur.
Hormonal method: an oral contraceptive supplies reproductive hormones.
These can inhibit egg maturation or ovulation, so an egg is not available for fertilisation.
Intrauterine method: an IUD is placed inside the uterus. Accept sterilisation blocking sperm ducts or oviducts as an alternative method.

The IUD can prevent implantation, impair sperm/fertilisation, or release hormones that thicken cervical mucus. For sterilisation: gametes cannot meet. Award this explanation mark only with the matching method. Do not credit abortion as contraception.
parts.note: Award up to 2 marks for each of three distinct methods; maximum 6.

questions.title: Inheritance of a recessive condition
questions.stem:
A recessive allele d causes a condition. Both parents have genotype Dd. The parents’ gametes are already arranged in this incomplete Punnett square:

parts.q: State the meaning of allele and genotype.
ms: Allele is a version of a gene (1).
Genotype is the combination of alleles an individual has (1).

parts.q: Complete Box A and Box B in the provided Punnett square.
ms: Box A = Dd (1).
Box B = Dd (1).

parts.q: Calculate the probability of an offspring having the condition. Give a percentage.
ms: Only dd has the condition; 1 of 4 (1).

parts.q: Explain why a dominant allele can be expressed in a heterozygous person, and why this does not mean it is always common in a population.
ms: Heterozygous means two different alleles (1).
One copy of a dominant allele is sufficient to affect phenotype (1).
Dominance describes expression, not how frequent an allele is (1).
Frequency also depends on inheritance, selection and chance/population history (1).

questions.title: Selection and biodiversity
questions.stem: Some beetles are green and some are brown. Birds find green beetles more easily on dark soil.

parts.q: State what is meant by variation and name one environmental cause of variation.
ms: Differences between individuals of a species (1).
Diet/light/exercise or another valid environmental factor (1).

parts.q: Explain how the proportion of brown beetles could increase over many generations.
ms: There is inherited variation in colour (1).
Brown beetles are less likely to be eaten (1).
More survive to reproduce (1).
They pass alleles for brown colour to offspring, increasing frequency (1).

parts.q: Give two reasons why a species may become extinct.
ms: Environmental change/habitat loss/new predator (one for 1).
New disease/competition/catastrophic event (a second distinct reason for 1).

parts.q: State two benefits of maintaining biodiversity.
ms: Helps maintain stable ecosystems/interdependence (1).
Preserves genetic resources/food/medicines or other valid ecosystem service (1).

questions.title: Sampling a field
questions.stem: Ten randomly placed quadrats each cover 0.25 m². A total of 60 daisies are counted. The field has area 200 m².

parts.q: Calculate the total area sampled.
Estimate the number of daisies in the field.
ms: Mean density = 60 / 2.5 (1).
24 daisies/m² (1).

parts.q: Describe how to place quadrats randomly.
ms: Set up numbered coordinates across the field (1).
Use random numbers to select positions (1).

parts.q: Explain two limitations of this estimate.
ms: Daisies may be unevenly distributed (1).
Small sampled fraction may not represent the whole field (1).
Counting/identification or seasonal differences can affect the estimate (1).

questions.title: Material cycles
questions.stem: Microorganisms break down dead leaves in a woodland. Water and carbon are continually recycled.

parts.q: Name the process by which plants remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and the process by which decomposers release it.
ms: Photosynthesis (1).
Respiration (1).

parts.q: Describe how water from the sea can return to the sea after falling on a woodland.
ms: Water evaporates from the sea and condenses to form clouds (1).
Precipitation/rain falls onto the woodland (1).
Water returns by surface runoff/rivers or groundwater flow (1).

parts.q: Describe how carbon from a leaf can return to a new tree.
ms: Decomposers break down leaf material (1).
Respiration releases carbon dioxide to atmosphere (1).
New tree absorbs carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, building biomass (1).

parts.q: Suggest two actions that reduce human impacts on biodiversity.
ms: Protect/restore habitats, such as reforestation (1).
Reduce pollution/waste, conservation breeding, or sustainable resource use (a second valid action for 1).

questions.title: Focusing on a book
questions.stem: A student looks from a distant tree to a nearby book. Light must be focused on the retina. Another student is short-sighted: distant light focuses in front of the retina.

parts.q: State the functions of the retina and optic nerve.
ms: The retina contains light-sensitive receptors.
The optic nerve carries impulses from the eye to the brain.

parts.q: Describe how the eye accommodates to the nearby book.
ms: Ciliary muscles contract.
Suspensory ligaments loosen.
The lens becomes thicker / refracts light more strongly.

parts.q: State how pupil size changes in bright light and explain its benefit.
ms: The pupil becomes smaller.
Less light enters, protecting the light-sensitive retina.

parts.q: Name the correcting lens for short sight and explain where corrected light should focus.
ms: Use a concave lens.
It refracts the light so the final image is focused on the retina.

parts.q: Give one alternative to spectacles for correcting a vision defect.
ms: Contact lenses, appropriate laser surgery or lens replacement.

questions.title: Treating kidney failure
questions.stem: A patient with kidney failure receives dialysis three times a week. A possible transplant would require a donor and medicines to reduce rejection.

parts.q: Name the organ that produces urea and the organ that removes it from blood.
ms: Urea is produced in the liver.
Kidneys remove it from blood.

parts.q: Name two useful substances normally reabsorbed by kidneys after filtration.
ms: Glucose.
An appropriate amount of water or ions.

parts.q: Describe the basic action of dialysis.
ms: Blood passes alongside dialysis fluid separated by a partially permeable membrane.
Urea moves from blood into dialysis fluid down a concentration gradient.
Blood cells and large proteins are retained.

parts.q: Compare a transplant with continuing dialysis.
ms: A successful transplant can give continuous function / avoid repeated dialysis sessions.
It requires a donor and has surgical / rejection risks.
Immune-suppressing medicines reduce rejection but increase infection risk.

questions.title: Light and seedling growth
questions.stem: Ten similar seedlings receive light from the left. Ten controls receive light equally from all sides. Both groups receive the same water, temperature and growing medium. After four days, shoots in the first group bend left.

parts.q: Name this directional growth response and explain the word positive.
ms: Phototropism.
Positive means growth towards the light stimulus.

parts.q: Explain why the evenly lit control group is useful.
ms: It provides a comparison without directional lighting.
A difference can therefore be linked more confidently to light direction.

parts.q: Give two measurements or records that improve the investigation.
ms: Measure shoot length / change in length.
Record direction using accurate labelled drawings or a consistent angle measure.

parts.q: Explain how plant hormones can cause bending.
ms: Unequal hormone / auxin distribution develops across the shoot.
The two sides grow at different rates.

parts.q: State the usual growth response of a root and shoot to gravity.
ms: Roots grow towards gravity / positive gravitropism.
Shoots grow against gravity / negative gravitropism.

questions.stem:

parts.q: Calculate the percentage increase in mean reaction time with distraction.
ms: Means 220 ms and 280 ms (1).
27.3% to 3 significant figures (1).

parts.q: Explain how an impulse crosses a synapse.
ms: Impulse triggers release of a neurotransmitter (1).
Chemical diffuses across gap (1).
Binds to receptors on next neurone and triggers a new electrical impulse (1).

parts.q: Compare nervous and hormonal coordination.
ms: Nervous signals travel along neurones; hormones are carried in blood (1).
Nervous responses generally faster/shorter lasting and more localised; hormonal responses generally slower/longer lasting (1).

parts.q: Suggest two ways to improve the validity of this comparison.
ms: Test same people in both conditions with order randomised (1).
Control sleep/caffeine/practice and other distractions, or use more participants (1).

questions.title: Negative feedback
questions.stem: A fasting person has falling blood glucose concentration. For the thyroxine question, use this information: the pituitary releases TSH, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroxine.

parts.q: Explain how glucagon restores blood glucose concentration.
ms: Pancreas detects low blood glucose/releases glucagon (1).
Glucagon travels to liver in blood (1).
Stimulates conversion of glycogen to glucose (1).
Glucose released into blood raises concentration (1).

parts.q: Explain why this is negative feedback.
ms: Response opposes the initial fall (1).
As concentration returns to normal, stimulation/glucagon secretion decreases (1).

parts.q: Explain how adrenaline prepares the body for action.
ms: Increases heart rate (1).
Increases delivery of oxygen and glucose to muscles for increased respiration (1).

parts.q: Explain how thyroxine secretion is controlled when its concentration becomes too high.
ms: High thyroxine inhibits pituitary release of TSH (1).
Less TSH stimulates thyroid, reducing thyroxine secretion (1).

questions.title: Reproductive hormone interactions
questions.stem: A clinic treats some cases of infertility with hormones. Success is not guaranteed.

parts.q: State the roles of FSH and LH during fertility treatment.
ms: FSH stimulates maturation of eggs (1).
LH stimulates ovulation/release of an egg (1).

parts.q: Explain how oestrogen and progesterone help regulate the menstrual cycle.
ms: Oestrogen stimulates rebuilding uterus lining (1).
Oestrogen inhibits FSH and stimulates LH release (1).
Progesterone maintains uterus lining (1).
Progesterone inhibits FSH and LH (1).

parts.q: A clinic reports 72 births from 240 treatment cycles. Calculate its birth rate per treatment cycle as a percentage.
Give one benefit and one risk or disadvantage of IVF.
ms: Can enable an infertile couple to have a child (1).
Multiple births/hormone side effects/emotional or financial cost; one valid disadvantage (1).

questions.title: Meiosis and inheritance
questions.stem: A recessive allele a causes a genetic condition. A carrier Aa has a child with a person aa who has the condition.

parts.q: Use a genetic cross to find the probability of a child having the condition. Give a decimal probability.
ms: Carrier gametes A and a; affected parent gamete a (1).
Offspring Aa and aa in equal proportions (1).
Probability 1/2 or 50% (1).

parts.q: Explain how meiosis and fertilisation maintain chromosome number across generations.
ms: Meiosis halves chromosome number in gametes (1).
Fertilisation joins/fuses two gamete nuclei (1).
Restores the full chromosome number in the zygote (1).

parts.q: Explain why siblings can have different phenotypes even with the same parents.
ms: Sexual reproduction produces different combinations of parental alleles (1).
Environmental differences can also affect phenotype (1).

parts.q: Evaluate using the result of this cross to predict the outcomes for exactly two children.
ms: Probability applies independently to each conception (1).
It does not guarantee that exactly one of two children will have the condition (1).

questions.title: Antibiotic resistance and genetic engineering
questions.stem: A hospital finds that an increasing proportion of bacteria are resistant to an antibiotic.

parts.q: Explain how resistance becomes more common and how prescribing decisions can slow this process.
ms: Random mutation creates an allele giving resistance/variation already exists.
Antibiotic creates a selection pressure.
Susceptible bacteria are killed.
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce rapidly.
Resistance allele is passed to offspring, increasing its frequency.
Prescribing antibiotics only when needed reduces selection pressure. Accept completion of the prescribed course as an alternative control, with a correct explanation.
parts.note: Award one mark per distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.

parts.q: Describe how bacteria can be genetically engineered to produce human insulin.
ms: Human insulin gene is isolated using enzymes (1).
Gene inserted into a vector/plasmid using enzymes (1).
Vector introduces gene into bacteria (1).
Modified bacteria are grown and express the gene to produce insulin, which is collected/purified (1).

questions.title: Interdependence and sampling
questions.stem: A field has area 800 m². Twenty 0.5 m² quadrats contain a total of 150 clover plants. Fewer clover plants are found near a shaded hedge.

parts.q: Estimate the total number of clover plants in the field.
ms: Area sampled = 20 x 0.5 = 10 m² (1).
Density = 150/10 = 15 plants/m² (1).
Estimate = 15 x 800 = 12000 plants (1).

parts.q: Design an investigation of the effect of distance from the hedge on clover abundance.
ms: Place a tape/transect perpendicular to hedge (1).
Sample quadrats at regular measured distances (1).
Count clover using a consistent inclusion rule and record light intensity/other relevant factor (1).
Repeat parallel transects and calculate mean abundance at each distance (1).

parts.q: Explain why the association with shade does not prove that light is the only cause.
ms: Other factors may vary with distance (1).
For example water/mineral availability/trampling/competition (1).
Need control or additional measurement/manipulation of these variables to test causation (1).

questions.title: Carbon and water cycles
questions.stem: A restoration project plants 400 trees. In a simplified model, each tree removes an average of 12 kg carbon dioxide per year. In practice, the value varies with tree age and environmental conditions.

parts.q: Calculate the total carbon dioxide removed per year in this model.
ms: 4800 kg per year (1).

parts.q: Explain how carbon from dead leaves can return to the atmosphere.
ms: Microorganisms/decomposers break down dead material (1).
Their respiration releases carbon dioxide (1).

parts.q: Explain how water is continually recycled between the sea, atmosphere and land.
ms: Evaporation from sea/land and transpiration from plants move water into air (1).
Water vapour condenses into clouds and falls as precipitation (1).
Runoff/rivers/groundwater return water to the sea (1).

parts.q: Explain how deforestation can increase atmospheric carbon dioxide.
ms: Fewer trees remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis (1).
Burning felled trees releases carbon dioxide (1).
Decay/respiration of dead biomass also releases carbon dioxide (1).

questions.title: Keeping warm and conserving water
questions.stem: A runner finishes training in cold dry air. Core temperature falls slightly and blood becomes more concentrated because water has been lost. No water is drunk immediately.

parts.q: Explain how shivering and vasoconstriction oppose the temperature fall.
ms: Shivering involves repeated muscle contraction and increased respiration.
Energy is transferred to thermal stores.
Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the skin.
This reduces energy transfer to the surroundings.

parts.q: Explain the ADH response to the more concentrated blood.
ms: A change in blood water concentration is detected in the brain.
The pituitary releases more ADH.
Kidney tubules become more permeable to water.
More water is reabsorbed into blood, producing a smaller volume of concentrated urine.

parts.q: Explain why this is negative feedback.
ms: The responses oppose the original change in water concentration.
As conditions return towards normal, the corrective ADH signal decreases.

questions.title: Researching a brain injury
questions.stem: A patient has impaired balance after a brain injury. MRI shows damage near the cerebellum. Researchers consider electrical stimulation during a clinically necessary procedure.

parts.q: State the normal function of the cerebellum and explain one limitation of linking the scan to the symptom.
ms: The cerebellum coordinates movement / balance.
Connected pathways may also be affected, so the symptom does not isolate one region’s function.

parts.q: Evaluate electrical stimulation as evidence for brain function.
ms: A reproducible response can link activation of a region to a function.
Complex connections mean stimulation may influence other regions.
Delicate brain tissue creates a risk of irreversible harm.
Informed consent and likely clinical benefit must justify the procedure.

parts.q: The patient looks from a near object to a distant one. Explain accommodation.
ms: Ciliary muscles relax.
Suspensory ligaments tighten.
The lens is pulled thinner.
It refracts light less strongly to focus the distant object on the retina.

questions.title: Assessing food-production choices
questions.stem: A farm’s feed contains 6000 kg dry biomass and its livestock gain 480 kg dry biomass. A proposed system reduces animal movement and controls temperature. The farm also considers replacing part of its output with fungal mycoprotein.

parts.q: Calculate biomass transfer efficiency.
ms: Efficiency = gain / input × 100.

parts.q: Explain two reasons the remaining input biomass does not become new livestock biomass.
ms: Some food is not digested and is egested.
Some absorbed material is lost through respiration / excretion, such as carbon dioxide, water or urea.

parts.q: Explain how the proposed livestock system could increase yield and give one drawback.
ms: Less movement reduces energy transferred in muscle activity.
Controlled temperature reduces energy demand for keeping warm.
A valid drawback concerns welfare, disease, cost or resource use.

parts.q: Explain one requirement for producing fungal mycoprotein and evaluate a potential benefit and limitation.
ms: A suitable carbohydrate supply, oxygen for aerobic growth or controlled temperature supports fungal growth in fermenters.
A valid benefit includes protein production with potentially less livestock demand.
A limitation such as energy / input costs, environmental impacts or consumer acceptance must be considered.

questions.title: Cells under the microscope
questions.stem: A student looks at cheek cells and a bacterium using images from a microscope.

parts.q: Name the part of a cheek cell where most aerobic respiration happens.
ms: Mitochondria/mitochondrion (1).

parts.q: Give two structures found in a bacterial cell that are not found in a cheek cell.
ms: Cell wall (1).
Plasmid / loop of DNA / flagellum (1).

parts.q: The image of a cheek cell is 30 mm wide. The real cell is 0.06 mm wide. Calculate the magnification.
Explain why an electron microscope shows more detail than a light microscope.
ms: Electron microscope has a higher resolution (1).
So can distinguish between two points closer together / see smaller structures such as ribosomes (1).

parts.q: A student says "Bacteria are bigger than animal cells." Use data to explain whether the student is correct. Typical bacterium: 2 μm. Typical cheek cell: 60 μm.
ms: Student is incorrect (1).
Cheek cell is 60 ÷ 2 = 30 times bigger (1).
About one order of magnitude larger (1).

questions.title: Cell division in a root tip
questions.stem: Cells in a root tip divide by mitosis.

parts.q: Give one reason why cells divide by mitosis.
ms: Growth / repair / replacement of cells (1).

parts.q: Describe what happens to the DNA before mitosis.
ms: It is copied / replicated (1).

parts.q: A root tip cell has 16 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does each daughter cell have after mitosis?
One cell divides by mitosis 4 times. Calculate how many cells are produced.
ms: 16 cells (1).

parts.q: Plant meristem cells are stem cells. Give two ways meristem cells can be used.
ms: Produce clones of plants quickly and cheaply (1).
Save rare species from extinction / produce crops with special features such as disease resistance (1).

parts.q: Explain why using embryonic stem cells in medicine is controversial.
ms: Embryos are destroyed (1).
Some people believe embryos have a right to life / religious objections (1).
Risk of viral infection/tumours from stem cells (1).

questions.title: Digesting a meal
questions.stem: A meal contains bread (starch), cheese (protein and fat) and an apple (sugar).

parts.q: Name the enzyme that digests starch.
ms: Amylase / carbohydrase (1).

parts.q: Name the products of fat digestion.
ms: Fatty acids (1).
Glycerol (1).

parts.q: Name the organ that produces bile.
ms: Liver (1).

parts.q: Describe how to test the bread for starch and give the positive result.
ms: Add iodine solution (1).
Turns blue-black (1).

parts.q: Explain why enzymes in the small intestine work best at a slightly alkaline pH, and how this pH is produced.
ms: Each enzyme has an optimum pH (1).
At other pH the active site changes shape / enzyme denatures (1).
Bile is alkaline (1).
Bile neutralises hydrochloric acid from the stomach (1).

questions.title: The heart and exercise
questions.stem: An athlete has a resting heart rate of 60 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 90 cm³.

parts.q: Calculate the athlete’s resting cardiac output in cm³ per minute.
ms: 5400 cm³/min (1).

parts.q: Name the blood vessel that carries blood from the left ventricle.
ms: Aorta (1).

parts.q: Name the part of the heart that controls the natural resting heart rate.
ms: Pacemaker (cells in the right atrium) (1).

parts.q: Give two ways the structure of a vein is different from an artery.
ms: Veins have thinner walls / less muscle (1).
Veins have valves / wider lumen (1).

parts.q: Explain how the alveoli are adapted for gas exchange.
ms: Large surface area (1).
Thin walls / one cell thick, short diffusion distance (1).
Good blood supply / many capillaries (1).
Maintain a steep concentration gradient / ventilation (1).

questions.title: Measles and vaccination
questions.stem: Measles is a disease caused by a virus.

parts.q: Give two symptoms of measles.
ms: Fever (1).
Red skin rash (1).

parts.q: Explain why measles cannot be treated with antibiotics.
ms: Antibiotics do not kill viruses (1).

parts.q: Describe how measles is spread.
ms: By inhalation of droplets from sneezes and coughs (1).

parts.q: Explain how vaccination prevents a child from becoming ill with measles.
ms: Vaccine contains dead/inactive measles virus or antigens (1).
White blood cells/lymphocytes are stimulated (1).
Specific antibodies are produced (1).
Memory cells remain in the blood (1).
On later infection, antibodies made quickly and in large amounts (1).
Virus destroyed before the child becomes ill (1).
parts.note: Award one mark for each distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.

questions.title: Photosynthesis in a leaf
questions.stem: Photosynthesis takes place in the leaves of plants.

parts.q: Complete the word equation: carbon dioxide + water → ______ + ______.
ms: Glucose (1).
Oxygen (1).

parts.q: Name the green substance that absorbs light.
ms: Chlorophyll (1).

parts.q: Give two ways a plant uses the glucose it makes.
ms: Respiration (1).
Making starch / cellulose / fats or oils / amino acids and proteins (1).

parts.q: A student finds the rate of photosynthesis increases as light intensity increases, up to a point, then stays the same. Explain why the rate stops increasing.
ms: Another factor becomes limiting (1).
Such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature (1).

parts.q: Explain why a farmer might heat a greenhouse in winter.
ms: Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes (1).
Low temperature slows enzyme activity / temperature is limiting (1).
Heating increases rate of photosynthesis, so faster growth/bigger yield (1).

questions.title: Yeast and bread
questions.stem: Bakers use yeast to make bread rise.

parts.q: Name the type of respiration yeast carries out without oxygen.
ms: Anaerobic respiration / fermentation (1).

parts.q: Complete the word equation: glucose → ______ + carbon dioxide.
ms: Ethanol (1).

parts.q: Explain why the bread rises.
ms: Carbon dioxide gas is produced (1).
Gas bubbles get trapped in the dough (1).

parts.q: A student measured the gas produced by yeast at different temperatures: 20 °C: 8 cm³; 30 °C: 22 cm³; 40 °C: 35 cm³; 60 °C: 2 cm³. All in 10 minutes. Calculate the mean rate at 40 °C in cm³ per minute.
ms: 3.5 cm³/min (1).

parts.q: Explain the result at 60 °C.
ms: Enzymes in the yeast are denatured (1).
Active site changes shape so respiration almost stops (1).

parts.q: Give two variables the student should control.
ms: Mass/concentration of yeast (1).
Concentration/volume of sugar solution / pH (1).

questions.title: Bacteria on agar
questions.stem: A student grows bacteria on an agar plate in a school laboratory.

parts.q: Give two steps the student should take to prevent contamination of the culture.
ms: Sterilise inoculating loop in a flame (1).
Lift the lid only slightly / sterilised Petri dishes and agar (1).

parts.q: Explain why the plate should be incubated at 25 °C.
ms: Lower temperature reduces the chance of growing pathogens (1).
Which grow best at body temperature, 37 °C (1).

parts.q: A clear zone around an antibiotic disc has a diameter of 12 mm. Calculate its area. Use π = 3.14.
ms: Radius = 6 mm (1).

parts.q: A bacterium divides every 30 minutes. Calculate how many bacteria are produced from one bacterium after 3 hours.
ms: 3 h = 6 divisions (1).
64 bacteria (1).

questions.title: Plants and water
questions.stem: A student uses a potometer to investigate water uptake by a leafy shoot.

parts.q: Name the tissue that carries water up the stem.
ms: Xylem (1).

parts.q: Name the pores in a leaf through which water vapour leaves.
ms: Stomata (1).

parts.q: The bubble moved 36 mm in 6 minutes. Calculate the rate in mm per minute.
ms: 6 mm/min (1).

parts.q: Predict and explain what would happen to the rate if a fan were turned on.
ms: Rate increases (1).
Water vapour is blown away from the leaf (1).
Steeper concentration gradient, so more diffusion/evaporation from stomata (1).

parts.q: Describe the role of guard cells.
ms: Guard cells open and close stomata (1).
When turgid, the stoma opens; when flaccid, it closes (1).
Controls gas exchange and water loss (1).

questions.title: A sick rose bush
questions.stem: A gardener notices that the leaves of a rose bush have purple-black spots and many leaves have fallen off.

parts.q: Name the disease and the type of pathogen that causes it.
ms: Rose black spot (1).
Fungus (1).

parts.q: Explain why the plant grows less well.
ms: Less photosynthesis due to fewer/damaged leaves (1).
So less glucose for growth (1).

parts.q: Suggest two ways the gardener could control the disease.
ms: Use fungicides (1).
Remove and burn affected leaves (1).

parts.q: Give one physical and one chemical defence that plants use against pathogens.
ms: Physical: cellulose cell walls / waxy cuticle / bark (1).
Chemical: antibacterial chemicals (1).

parts.q: A different plant has yellow leaves. Suggest a mineral deficiency that could cause this and explain why.
ms: Magnesium deficiency (1).
Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll (1).

questions.title: Surface area and diffusion
questions.stem: Agar cubes containing a pink indicator are placed in acid. The pink colour disappears as acid diffuses in.

parts.q: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a 2 cm cube. Give your answer as x : 1.
Predict and explain which cube, 1 cm or 3 cm, will lose its colour completely first.
ms: 1 cm cube (1).
Larger SA:V (1).
Shorter distance for acid to diffuse to the centre (1).

parts.q: Explain why an elephant needs a transport system but an amoeba does not.
ms: Elephant has a small SA:V (1).
Diffusion distance to cells is too long/slow (1).
Amoeba has a large SA:V so diffusion through the membrane is enough (1).

parts.q: Give two features of the fish gill that make gas exchange efficient.
ms: Large surface area of filaments/lamellae (1).
Thin lamellae / good blood supply / counter-current flow (1).

questions.title: Transport across membranes
questions.stem: Root hair cells absorb water and mineral ions from the soil.

parts.q: Explain how water enters root hair cells.
ms: By osmosis (1).
From dilute soil water to more concentrated cell contents, through a partially permeable membrane (1).

parts.q: Explain why root hair cells need many mitochondria.
ms: Mineral ions absorbed by active transport (1).
Against a concentration gradient (1).
Needs energy released by respiration in mitochondria (1).

parts.q: A potato cylinder changed from 3.20 g to 2.88 g in sugar solution. Calculate the percentage change in mass.
Explain the result in terms of osmosis.
ms: Sugar solution more concentrated than cell contents (1).
Water moved out of the cells by osmosis (1).
Through a partially permeable membrane, so mass decreased (1).

questions.title: Enzyme investigation
questions.stem: A student investigated the effect of pH on the time taken for amylase to digest starch. pH 5: 180 s; pH 6: 60 s; pH 7: 40 s; pH 8: 90 s.

parts.q: Calculate the rate at pH 7 using rate = 1000 ÷ time.
Suggest the optimum pH and explain how the student could find it more precisely.
ms: Optimum around pH 7 (1).
Test pH values in smaller intervals between 6 and 8 (1).

parts.q: Explain why the rate is lower at pH 5.
ms: pH changes the shape of the active site (1).
Starch fits less well / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes (1).
So digestion slower (1).

parts.q: Give two variables the student should control and explain why a water bath is used.
ms: Temperature (1).
Volume/concentration of starch or amylase (1).
Water bath keeps temperature constant so only pH affects the rate (1).

questions.title: Cardiovascular disease
questions.stem: Coronary heart disease is a leading cause of death in the UK.

parts.q: Explain how a build-up of fatty material in coronary arteries can lead to a heart attack.
ms: Arteries narrow, reducing blood flow (1).
Less oxygen reaches heart muscle (1).
Heart muscle cannot respire / cells die (1).

parts.q: Describe how a stent works.
ms: Mesh tube inserted to hold the artery open (1).

parts.q: Evaluate the use of statins and stents to treat coronary heart disease.
ms: Statins reduce blood cholesterol and slow fatty deposits (1).
Statins are non-surgical / reduce risk long-term (1).
Statins must be taken for life / take time / possible side effects (1).
Stents work immediately to restore blood flow (1).
Stent insertion has risks of surgery, infection, clots / artery may narrow again (1).
Justified conclusion, e.g. both used together (1).
parts.note: Award one mark for each distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.

questions.title: Monoclonal antibodies
questions.stem: Monoclonal antibodies can be used to diagnose and treat disease.

parts.q: Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced.
ms: Mouse injected with antigen so lymphocytes make the antibody (1).
Lymphocytes collected and fused with tumour cells (1).
Forming hybridoma cells (1).
Hybridoma cloned; antibodies collected and purified (1).

parts.q: Explain how a monoclonal antibody can deliver a drug to cancer cells only.
ms: Antibody is specific to an antigen on cancer cells (1).
Drug attached to the antibody (1).
Antibody binds only to cancer cells, so healthy cells are not harmed (1).

parts.q: Give one disadvantage of using monoclonal antibodies.
ms: More side effects than expected / expensive (1).

parts.q: Explain why monoclonal antibodies can be used in pregnancy tests.
ms: They bind specifically to the hormone hCG (1).
hCG is only present in urine during pregnancy (1).

questions.title: Limiting factors
questions.stem: A grower investigated how light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration affect the rate of photosynthesis in tomato plants.

parts.q: A lamp gives a light intensity of 120 units at 10 cm. Calculate the intensity at 30 cm.
At high light, rate was 18 units at 0.04% CO₂ and 28 units at 0.1% CO₂. Explain what this shows.
ms: Carbon dioxide was limiting at 0.04% (1).
Increasing CO₂ increased the rate (1).

parts.q: Explain why increasing temperature above 40 °C reduces the rate of photosynthesis.
ms: Photosynthesis is catalysed by enzymes (1).
Above the optimum, enzymes denature (1).
Active site changes shape, so fewer reactions (1).

parts.q: The grower spends £400 a week on extra CO₂ and earns £550 more from the increased crop. Calculate the change in profit and comment.
ms: Worthwhile while CO₂ is limiting; no benefit if another factor limits (1).

questions.title: Oxygen debt
questions.stem: An athlete runs a 400 m race. Her oxygen uptake was 0.3 dm³/min at rest and averaged 1.5 dm³/min for 6 minutes after the race.

parts.q: Calculate the oxygen debt.
Explain why the athlete has an oxygen debt.
ms: During the race, oxygen supply was not enough for aerobic respiration (1).
Muscles respired anaerobically (1).
Lactic acid built up (1).
Extra oxygen needed afterwards to convert lactic acid to glucose in the liver (1).

parts.q: Explain why heart rate remains high after exercise.
ms: To transport lactic acid to the liver (1).
To deliver oxygen to repay the oxygen debt (1).

parts.q: Give two ways glucose is used in metabolism other than respiration.
ms: Converted to glycogen / starch / cellulose (1).
Used to make lipids or (with nitrate) amino acids/proteins (1).

questions.title: Testing a new drug
questions.stem: A new drug for high blood pressure is being developed.

parts.q: Explain why the drug is first tested on cells and animals.
ms: To check for toxicity/safety (1).
And efficacy before testing on humans (1).

parts.q: In a trial, 150 of 500 patients given the drug and 60 of 500 given a placebo showed reduced blood pressure. Calculate the percentage in each group.
ms: Placebo: 12% (1).

parts.q: Explain why the trial was double-blind.
ms: Neither doctors nor patients know who has the drug (1).
Removes bias in reporting or assessment (1).

parts.q: Explain why the results should be peer reviewed before the drug is used.
ms: Other scientists check the method and results (1).
To check results are valid / not biased / can be reproduced (1).

parts.q: Suggest why the trial used 1000 patients rather than 20.
ms: Larger sample reduces the effect of random variation (1).
Results more representative / rare side effects more likely to be detected (1).

questions.title: Comparing disinfectants
questions.stem: Three disinfectants were tested on a lawn of bacteria. Clear zone diameters: A 8 mm, B 16 mm, C 0 mm.

parts.q: Calculate the area of the clear zone for B. Use π = 3.14.
Calculate how many times larger the area for B is than for A.
Explain why a disc soaked in sterile water was included.
ms: It is a control (1).
To show any clear zone is caused by the disinfectant, not the disc (1).

parts.q: Explain why the lid should be taped at only two points and the plate not opened after incubation.
ms: Allows oxygen in so harmful anaerobic bacteria do not grow (1).
Prevents release of possible pathogens (1).

parts.q: Suggest one reason why disinfectant C produced no clear zone.
ms: Bacteria are resistant to C / C is ineffective (1).
Or C did not diffuse into the agar / concentration too low (1).

questions.title: Diagnosing crop disease
questions.stem: A farmer’s wheat crop has stunted plants and discoloured leaves.

parts.q: Suggest two ways the farmer could identify whether the cause is a pathogen.
ms: Send samples to a laboratory to identify the pathogen (1).
Use a testing kit containing monoclonal antibodies (1).

parts.q: Stunted growth can be caused by nitrate deficiency. Explain why.
ms: Nitrate is needed to make amino acids/protein (1).
Protein is needed for growth (1).

parts.q: Aphids are found on the crop. Explain how aphids can damage the plants.
ms: Aphids feed on phloem sap / sugars (1).
Can transmit viruses (1).

parts.q: Describe two mechanical adaptations plants use to deter animals.
ms: Thorns/hairs (1).
Leaves that droop/curl when touched / mimicry (1).

parts.q: Explain how a plant can reduce the spread of a pathogen after a leaf has been infected.
ms: Leaf is dropped / dead cells fall off (1).
So the pathogen is removed before it spreads / antibacterial chemicals produced (1).

questions.title: The nervous system
questions.stem: A person steps on a pin and quickly lifts their foot.

parts.q: What type of response is this?
ms: Reflex (1).

parts.q: Name the receptor and the effector in this response.
ms: Receptor: pain receptor in skin (1).
Effector: muscle (in leg) (1).

parts.q: Put these in the correct order: motor neurone, receptor, relay neurone, effector, sensory neurone.
ms: Receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (1).
→ motor neurone → effector (1).

parts.q: Explain why this type of response is important.
ms: It is fast/automatic (1).
Protects the body from damage (1).

parts.q: Describe how a nerve impulse passes across a synapse.
ms: Impulse arrives and a chemical is released (1).
Chemical diffuses across the gap (1).
Triggers a new impulse in the next neurone (1).

questions.title: Diabetes
questions.stem: Blood glucose concentration must be kept within narrow limits.

parts.q: Name the organ that monitors blood glucose concentration.
ms: Pancreas (1).

parts.q: Name the hormone released when blood glucose concentration is too high.
ms: Insulin (1).

parts.q: Describe the effect of this hormone.
ms: Glucose moves from the blood into cells (1).
Liver and muscles convert glucose to glycogen for storage (1).

parts.q: Give two differences between type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
ms: Type 1: no/little insulin made; type 2: cells do not respond to insulin (1).
Type 1 treated with insulin injections; type 2 with diet/exercise (1).

parts.q: Data: 4% of adults with a normal weight and 14% of adults who are obese have type 2 diabetes. Calculate how many times more likely obese adults are to have type 2 diabetes.
ms: 3.5 times (1).

parts.q: Explain why this data does not prove that obesity causes type 2 diabetes.
ms: Correlation does not prove causation (1).
Other factors such as age, diet, exercise or genes may be involved (1).

questions.title: Body temperature
questions.stem: A student runs on a hot day.

parts.q: Name the part of the brain that monitors body temperature.
ms: Thermoregulatory centre / hypothalamus (1).

parts.q: Give two ways the body responds to an increase in core temperature.
ms: More sweat released (1).
Blood vessels supplying skin capillaries dilate (1).

parts.q: Explain how one of these responses cools the body.
ms: Sweat evaporates (1).
Using energy from the skin (1).

parts.q: Explain why it is important that core body temperature stays at about 37 °C.
ms: This is the optimum temperature for enzymes (1).
Enzymes denature if too hot / reactions slow if too cold (1).

parts.q: Describe how the body responds if core temperature falls too low.
ms: Shivering: muscles contract, respiration releases energy (1).
Vasoconstriction: less blood flows near the skin (1).
Less sweat produced (1).

questions.title: Inheriting eye colour
questions.stem: In a simplified model, brown eyes (B) are dominant to blue eyes (b).

parts.q: What is the genotype of a person with blue eyes?
Give two possible genotypes of a person with brown eyes.
ms: BB and Bb (1).

parts.q: Two parents are both Bb. Draw a Punnett square to show the possible offspring.
ms: Gametes B and b from each parent (1).
Offspring BB, Bb, Bb, bb (1).
Correctly laid out grid (1).

parts.q: Give the probability that their child has blue eyes.
What is the term for a person with two different alleles?
ms: Heterozygous (1).

parts.q: Explain why a child has a 50% chance of being male.
ms: Mother gives X in every egg (1).
Father gives X or Y in equal numbers of sperm (1).
So XX and XY are equally likely (1).

questions.title: Variation and evolution
questions.stem: Peppered moths can be pale or dark.

parts.q: Name the process that produced the first dark moth.
ms: Mutation (1).

parts.q: In polluted areas, dark moths became more common. Explain why, using natural selection.
ms: Variation exists: some moths are dark (1).
Dark moths camouflaged on soot-covered trees (1).
Fewer dark moths eaten by birds (1).
Dark moths survive and reproduce (1).
Pass on the allele for dark colour (1).
Over generations the proportion of dark moths increases (1).
parts.note: Award one mark for each distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.

parts.q: Give two causes of variation between individuals of the same species.
ms: Genetic / genes inherited (1).
Environment (1).

parts.q: What is meant by a species?
ms: A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring (1).

questions.title: Selective breeding and cloning
questions.stem: A farmer wants to produce cows that give more milk.

parts.q: Describe how the farmer could use selective breeding.
ms: Choose cows that produce most milk and a bull from a high-yield line (1).
Breed them together (1).
Select best offspring and repeat over many generations (1).

parts.q: Give one problem caused by selective breeding.
ms: Inbreeding / reduced variation / inherited defects (1).

parts.q: Embryo transplants can be used to produce many identical calves. Describe how.
ms: Cells removed from an early embryo before they specialise (1).
Split into several embryos (1).
Implanted into host mothers (1).

parts.q: Give two advantages of using cuttings to produce new plants.
ms: Quick/cheap (1).
Plants are identical so keep desirable features (1).

parts.q: Give one disadvantage of cloning crops.
ms: Little variation, so disease could affect all plants (1).

questions.title: Investigating a habitat
questions.stem: A class estimates the number of daisies on the school field. The field is 80 m by 50 m.

parts.q: Describe how the class should place their quadrats.
ms: Randomly (1).
Using random coordinates on a grid of tape measures (1).

parts.q: The mean number of daisies in a 1 m² quadrat is 3.5. Estimate the number of daisies in the field.
ms: Area = 4000 m² (1).

parts.q: Explain why the class should use many quadrats.
ms: Gives a more representative sample (1).
Reduces effect of anomalies / more reliable mean (1).

parts.q: Name one abiotic factor that could affect the distribution of daisies.
ms: Light intensity / soil moisture / soil pH / temperature (1).

parts.q: Describe how the class could find out how daisy numbers change from under a tree to the open field.
ms: Use a transect line from tree to field (1).
Place quadrats at regular intervals and count daisies (1).

questions.title: Food chains and pollution
questions.stem: A pond contains algae, water fleas, small fish and herons.

parts.q: Write a food chain for this pond.
ms: algae → water fleas → small fish → herons (1).
Arrows point from food to consumer (1).

parts.q: Name the producer.
ms: Algae (1).

parts.q: Fertiliser washes into the pond. Explain why fish may die.
ms: Algae grow rapidly and block light (1).
Plants below cannot photosynthesise and die (1).
Bacteria decompose dead plants and use up oxygen (1).
Fish cannot get enough oxygen (1).

parts.q: Give two ways people reduce biodiversity.
ms: Deforestation / habitat destruction (1).
Pollution / climate change from burning fossil fuels (1).

parts.q: Give one benefit of maintaining high biodiversity.
ms: More stable ecosystem / resources such as medicines and food (1).

questions.title: Focusing on near and far objects
questions.stem: A student reads a book, then looks out of the window at a distant tree.

parts.q: Name the part of the eye that contains light receptors.
ms: Retina (1).

parts.q: Name the part of the eye that controls the size of the pupil.
ms: Iris (1).

parts.q: Describe how the eye focuses on the distant tree.
ms: Ciliary muscles relax (1).
Suspensory ligaments tighten (1).
Lens becomes thinner, refracting light less (1).

parts.q: Some people are short-sighted. Explain what this means and how it is corrected.
ms: Cannot see distant objects clearly (1).
Light focuses in front of the retina (1).
Corrected with a concave lens (1).

parts.q: Give one risk of laser eye surgery.
ms: Infection / damage to the cornea (1).
Vision may be worse / may need further treatment (1).

questions.title: Waste and recycling
questions.stem: The body and ecosystems both need to remove or recycle waste.

parts.q: Name the waste product made in the liver from excess amino acids.
ms: Urea (1).

parts.q: Name the organ that removes this waste from the blood.
ms: Kidney (1).

parts.q: Explain why the dialysis fluid contains the same concentration of glucose as normal blood.
ms: No concentration gradient for glucose (1).
So glucose does not diffuse out of the blood (1).

parts.q: Give two disadvantages of dialysis compared with a kidney transplant.
ms: Several sessions a week / time-consuming (1).
Restricted diet / expensive long-term / risk of infection (1).

parts.q: Give three conditions that speed up decay in a compost heap.
ms: Warmth (1).
Moisture (1).
Oxygen / turning the heap (1).

parts.q: Name the gas made by anaerobic decay in a biogas generator.
ms: Methane (1).

questions.title: Investigating reaction time
questions.stem: Students used a ruler-drop test to investigate whether caffeine-free and caffeinated drinks affect reaction time. Mean catch distance before: 18.0 cm; after caffeine: 12.6 cm.

parts.q: Calculate the percentage decrease in mean catch distance.
Give two variables the students should control.
ms: Same hand / same person dropping / same ruler (1).
Same starting position / same volume of drink / same time after drinking (1).

parts.q: Explain why a placebo drink was given to a second group.
ms: To check the effect is caused by caffeine (1).
Not by expectation or practice (1).

parts.q: Explain why reaction time is limited by synapses.
ms: Transmission at synapses involves chemical diffusion (1).
This is slower than electrical impulses along neurones (1).

parts.q: Suggest one ethical issue with this investigation.
ms: Caffeine may harm some participants (1).
Need informed consent / right to withdraw (1).

questions.title: Negative feedback
questions.stem: The thyroid gland releases thyroxine.

parts.q: Describe the role of thyroxine.
ms: Controls/stimulates basal metabolic rate (1).
Important in growth and development (1).

parts.q: Explain how thyroxine levels are controlled by negative feedback.
ms: When thyroxine is low, the pituitary releases TSH (1).
TSH stimulates the thyroid to release thyroxine (1).
When thyroxine is high, TSH release is inhibited (1).
So thyroxine is kept within a narrow range (1).

parts.q: Explain why glucagon is needed when a person has not eaten for several hours.
ms: Blood glucose falls, detected by the pancreas (1).
Pancreas secretes glucagon (1).
Glucagon causes the liver to convert glycogen into glucose (1).
Glucose released into the blood, raising its level (1).

questions.title: Water balance
questions.stem: A hiker loses a lot of water by sweating.

parts.q: Name the hormone that controls the water content of the blood and the gland that releases it.
ms: ADH (1).
Pituitary gland (1).

parts.q: Explain how this hormone helps the hiker conserve water.
ms: Blood becomes more concentrated, detected in the brain (1).
More ADH released (1).
Kidney tubules more permeable to water (1).
More water reabsorbed into blood; small volume of concentrated urine (1).

parts.q: Explain why urine normally contains no glucose.
ms: Glucose is filtered out of the blood (1).
All glucose is reabsorbed (1).

parts.q: Explain why ammonia is converted into urea.
ms: Ammonia is toxic (1).
Urea is less toxic / safer to transport and excrete (1).

questions.title: IVF treatment
questions.stem: A couple are having IVF treatment.

parts.q: Explain why the woman is given FSH and LH.
ms: FSH causes eggs to mature (1).
LH causes egg release, so several eggs can be collected (1).

parts.q: Describe the stages of IVF after the eggs are collected.
ms: Eggs fertilised by sperm in the laboratory (1).
Fertilised eggs develop into embryos (1).
One or two embryos are inserted into the uterus (1).

parts.q: A clinic had 210 successful births from 750 treatment cycles. Calculate the success rate.
Give three concerns about IVF.
ms: Low success rate / expensive (1).
Emotionally and physically stressful (1).
Multiple births are risky / unused embryos destroyed (1).

questions.title: DNA and protein synthesis
questions.stem: A gene codes for an enzyme.

parts.q: A section of the coding strand has 450 bases. Calculate the number of amino acids it codes for.
In a DNA molecule, 22% of the bases are thymine. Calculate the percentage of cytosine.
Describe how the enzyme is made from the gene.
ms: Template copy of gene made in nucleus and moves to a ribosome (1).
Carrier molecules bring amino acids (1).
Amino acids joined in the order set by base triplets (1).
Chain folds into a specific shape (1).

parts.q: Explain how a mutation could stop the enzyme working.
ms: Mutation changes the base sequence / a triplet (1).
Different amino acid in the chain, so protein folds differently (1).
Active site changes shape, substrate no longer fits (1).

questions.title: Inherited disorders
questions.stem: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is caused by a recessive allele, f.

parts.q: A man who is a carrier and a woman with cystic fibrosis have children. Use a Punnett square to find the probability that a child has CF.
ms: Parents Ff and ff give offspring Ff, Ff, ff, ff (1).

parts.q: Explain why two parents without CF can have a child with CF.
ms: Both parents are carriers / heterozygous Ff (1).
Each passes on f, so the child is ff (1).

parts.q: Evaluate screening embryos for cystic fibrosis.
ms: Embryos produced by IVF are tested for the CF allele (1).
Only embryos without CF are implanted (1).
Reduces suffering / cost of lifelong treatment (1).
Expensive / possible errors (1).
Embryos destroyed — ethical objections (1).
Concern about designer babies / implies less value of people with CF; conclusion (1).
parts.note: Award one mark for each distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.

questions.title: Evolution and classification
questions.stem: Scientists compare the DNA of several primate species.

parts.q: Explain how DNA evidence can show how closely related two species are.
ms: Similar DNA base sequences (1).
More similar sequence means a more recent common ancestor (1).

parts.q: Give two reasons why Darwin’s theory was not widely accepted at first.
ms: Challenged belief that God created all life (1).
Insufficient evidence / mechanism of inheritance unknown (1).

parts.q: Explain how geographical isolation can lead to the formation of a new species.
ms: Populations separated by a barrier, e.g. river or mountain (1).
No interbreeding between populations (1).
Mutations give different alleles in each population (1).
Different conditions select different characteristics (1).
Natural selection over many generations changes allele frequencies (1).
Eventually cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring — new species (1).
parts.note: Award one mark for each distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.

questions.title: Biomass and food chains
questions.stem: A field of grass contains 30 000 kg of biomass. Cattle feeding on the grass contain 2400 kg of biomass.

parts.q: Calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer from grass to cattle.
Give three reasons why not all the biomass of the grass is transferred to the cattle.
ms: Not all grass is eaten, e.g. roots (1).
Some is not digested and is egested in faeces (1).
Glucose used in respiration / lost as CO₂ and water / urea (1).

parts.q: Explain why it is more efficient for humans to eat plants rather than meat.
ms: Biomass is lost at each trophic level (1).
Fewer levels so more biomass available to humans (1).

parts.q: Evaluate keeping cattle indoors in small pens to increase meat production.
ms: Less movement and warmth means less energy lost, so more growth (1).
Ethical concerns about animal welfare (1).
Disease spreads easily, so more antibiotic use / cost of heating (1).

questions.title: Decay investigation
questions.stem: A student investigated decay of milk at different temperatures using lipase and phenolphthalein indicator. Time for colour change: 20 °C 500 s; 30 °C 250 s; 40 °C 125 s; 60 °C no change.

parts.q: Explain why the indicator changes colour.
ms: Lipase breaks down fat into fatty acids (1).
pH falls so phenolphthalein turns from pink to colourless (1).

parts.q: Calculate the rate at 30 °C using rate = 1000 ÷ time.
Describe the pattern between 20 °C and 40 °C.
ms: Rate doubles for every 10 °C rise (1).
Time halves from 500 to 250 to 125 s (1).

parts.q: Explain why there was no colour change at 60 °C.
ms: Lipase denatured (1).
Active site changes shape so fat is not broken down (1).

parts.q: Explain why gardeners turn compost heaps.
ms: Adds oxygen (1).
Decomposers respire aerobically (1).
So decay is faster (1).

questions.title: Food security
questions.stem: The world population is increasing, so food security is a global concern.

parts.q: Give two factors that threaten food security.
ms: Increasing population / changing diets (1).
New pests and pathogens / drought / cost of inputs / conflict (1).

parts.q: Explain how fishing quotas and larger net mesh sizes help to maintain fish stocks.
ms: Quotas limit the number of fish caught (1).
So enough fish remain to breed (1).
Larger mesh lets young fish escape (1).
They reach breeding age and reproduce (1).

parts.q: Describe how mycoprotein is produced.
ms: Fusarium fungus grown in a fermenter (1).
On glucose syrup as food (1).
Aerobic conditions with controlled temperature and pH (1).
Fungal biomass harvested and purified (1).
